slides.title: Sodium (Na)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: A routine test of general health that helps find and monitor conditions affecting the balance of fluids, electrolytes and acidity. It is often done as part of an electrolyte panel or a basic (BMP) or comprehensive (CMP) metabolic panel.

It may be ordered at a routine checkup, in people taking medicines that can affect fluid balance, or when there are symptoms of high sodium (thirst, passing very little urine) or low sodium (weakness, fatigue). Confusion, muscle twitching and seizures can occur with both.

slides.title: Sodium (Na)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Sodium is often measured with other electrolytes for the anion gap test, which looks at the difference between negatively and positively charged electrolytes and helps check for acid imbalances.

Physiology: Sodium is an electrolyte: it helps control the amount of body fluid and the acid–base (pH) balance, and helps nerves and muscles work properly. Most sodium comes from the diet; the kidneys excrete any excess in urine, and blood sodium is normally kept within a very narrow range.

slides.title: Sodium (Na)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: Possible causes of a higher-than-normal result include dehydration (from not drinking enough, diarrhea or diuretic medicines), adrenal gland disorders, kidney disease and, uncommonly, diabetes insipidus.

Low: Possible causes include sodium loss through diarrhea or vomiting, and conditions in which the body holds onto extra fluid that dilutes sodium: kidney disease, cirrhosis of the liver, heart failure, certain brain and lung diseases, some cancers and certain medicines (including many over-the-counter pain relievers and some antidepressants). Addison disease and malnutrition are also listed.

slides.title: Sodium (Na)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines being taken; some may need to be stopped before the test, but only on the provider’s instruction. Fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

Limitations: A result outside the normal range does not always mean a condition that needs treatment: certain medicines, age, sex and some medical conditions can raise or lower sodium. For diagnosis, the result is usually considered together with other tests, such as other electrolytes.

slides.title: Potassium (K)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)

What it is used for: Often part of a routine electrolyte panel; used to diagnose or monitor conditions linked to abnormal potassium, such as kidney disease, high blood pressure and heart disease. It is also used to monitor diabetes, kidney disease or adrenal gland disorders and people taking medicines that can affect potassium.

Physiology: Potassium is an electrolyte that cells, nerves, the heart and muscles need to work properly. Almost all body potassium is inside cells, with only a small amount in the blood; the kidneys remove potassium in urine to keep the blood level right.

slides.title: Potassium (K)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Interpreting the result · 1/2
cols: High potassium (hyperkalemia) often has two or more causes.

Possible causes of low potassium (hypokalemia) include side effects of prescription diuretics, fluid loss from diarrhea, vomiting or heavy sweating, laxative overuse, adrenal gland disorders (Cushing’s syndrome, aldosteronism), kidney disease, alcohol use disorder and, uncommonly, a diet too low in potassium.

slides.title: Potassium (K)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Interpreting the result · 2/2
cols: Possibilities include kidney disease, Addison disease, injuries, burns or surgery (which make cells release extra potassium), poorly controlled type 1 diabetes, side effects of certain medicines such as diuretics or antibiotics and, uncommonly, a very high potassium intake from food or supplements.

slides.title: Potassium (K)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a potassium test or an electrolyte panel. Fasting for several hours may be needed if other tests are ordered on the same blood sample.
Interferences: Repeatedly clenching and relaxing the fist just before or during blood collection can temporarily raise blood potassium and lead to an incorrect result.

Certain prescription and over-the-counter medicines and supplements may raise potassium. Natural black licorice should not be eaten for at least two weeks before the test because it may lower potassium.

slides.title: Potassium (K)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: A result outside the normal range does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Chloride (Cl⁻)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)

What it is used for: Usually measured in routine blood screening, often in an electrolyte panel together with potassium, sodium and bicarbonate. It helps monitor or diagnose acid or fluid imbalances and, with other electrolytes, conditions such as kidney disease, heart failure, liver disease and high blood pressure.
Urine also contains some chloride, and a urine chloride test may be recommended to get more information about chloride levels.

slides.title: Chloride (Cl⁻)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Chloride is an electrolyte obtained from food, mainly from salt; the excess is removed in urine. It helps control the amount of fluid in the body and helps maintain healthy blood volume and blood pressure.

slides.title: Chloride (Cl⁻)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Interpreting the result
cols: High chloride (hyperchloremia) may be a sign of dehydration, kidney disease or metabolic acidosis, a condition with too much acid in the blood.

Low chloride (hypochloremia) may be a sign of heart failure, lung disease, Addison disease (the adrenal glands do not make enough of certain hormones) or metabolic alkalosis, a condition with too much base in the blood.

slides.title: Chloride (Cl⁻)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines; some may need to be stopped before the test, but only on the provider’s instruction. Fasting for several hours may be needed if other blood tests are ordered.
Interferences: Drinking too much fluid, losing fluid through vomiting or diarrhea, and certain medicines such as antacids can affect chloride levels and cause abnormal results.
Limitations: A chloride result outside the normal range does not always mean a medical problem that needs treatment; many diseases and other factors can change chloride.

slides.title: Calcium (Ca)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used to check general health and to help diagnose or monitor conditions affecting the bones, kidneys, digestive system, thyroid and parathyroid glands. Total calcium is the most common blood calcium test and is often part of the BMP and CMP.

Ionized calcium is harder to measure; it is usually ordered when total calcium is abnormal, when a condition affects the balance of ionized and bound calcium, or in people who are seriously ill or having surgery.

slides.title: Calcium (Ca)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Many people with high or low calcium have no symptoms, so the test may be ordered in known conditions that can affect calcium, such as kidney disease, thyroid or parathyroid disease, malnutrition, problems absorbing calcium and certain cancers.

Physiology: About 1% of the body’s calcium is in the blood; the rest is stored in bones and teeth. The right blood calcium level is needed for nerves, muscles and the heart to work properly; calcium also helps blood vessels move blood and helps release hormones.

slides.title: Calcium (Ca)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Blood calcium exists in two forms normally present in about equal amounts: calcium bound to proteins and free (ionized) calcium, the form active in many body functions. Because the body tightly controls their balance, total calcium usually gives a good estimate of ionized calcium.

slides.title: Calcium (Ca)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Interpreting the result
cols: Possible causes of high total calcium (hypercalcemia) include overactive parathyroid glands (hyperparathyroidism), certain cancers including cancer that has spread to bone, bone disorders such as Paget’s disease of bone, and taking too much vitamin D over a long period.

Possible causes of low total calcium (hypocalcemia) include low blood protein levels (for example from liver disease or malnutrition), underactive parathyroid glands (hypoparathyroidism), too little dietary calcium, too little vitamin D or magnesium, pancreatitis and kidney disease.

slides.title: Calcium (Ca)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: Usually no special preparation is needed. Tell the provider about all medicines and supplements, such as vitamin D, as some may need to be stopped (only on the provider’s instruction); fasting may be needed if other tests are ordered on the sample.
Interferences: Diet and certain medicines can affect calcium levels, so a total calcium result outside the normal range does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.
Limitations: A blood calcium test does not show how much calcium is in the bones; bone mineral content is measured with a bone density (DEXA) scan.

slides.title: Magnesium (Mg)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)

What it is used for: Done when abnormal magnesium is suspected. Low magnesium (hypomagnesemia) is more common than high; high magnesium (hypermagnesemia) is uncommon and occurs mostly in kidney failure. The test may also help find the cause of abnormal calcium, potassium and phosphorus, because magnesium plays a role in how these are absorbed.

slides.title: Magnesium (Mg)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Monitoring may be needed in chronic kidney disease, poorly controlled diabetes, alcohol use disorder, malabsorption syndrome, malnutrition, chronic diarrhea, low potassium and/or calcium, or during treatment with magnesium and/or calcium. It is also checked in people taking medicines that can lower magnesium (diuretics, certain antibiotics, proton pump inhibitors) or raise it (aspirin, magnesium-containing laxatives or antacids, lithium).

Physiology: Magnesium is a mineral and electrolyte obtained from many foods. The body needs it for muscle, nerve and heart function; it also helps control blood pressure and blood glucose, is important for strong bones and supports the immune system.

slides.title: Magnesium (Mg)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Most body magnesium is stored in bones, organs and other tissues; only a small amount is in the blood. Blood levels are tightly controlled mainly by the kidneys, which limit urinary loss when magnesium is low, and by the intestines, which control absorption from food.

slides.title: Magnesium (Mg)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: High magnesium may result from too much magnesium from dietary supplements, laxatives, antacids or certain prescription medicines (rarely from food alone) or from a problem getting rid of magnesium, most commonly kidney failure. Dehydration, hypothyroidism, Addison disease and overactive parathyroid glands are also linked.

Low: Low magnesium may result from too little dietary intake (more likely in older adults and people with alcohol use disorder or malnutrition), poor absorption (e.g. digestive disorders such as Crohn’s disease, or certain medicines) or excessive loss (kidney problems, long-term diarrhea, or diabetes with high blood glucose causing frequent urination). Underactive parathyroid glands and pregnancy are also linked.

slides.title: Magnesium (Mg)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: Usually no preparation is needed; fasting for several hours may be required if other blood tests are done at the same time. Tell the provider about all prescription and over-the-counter medicines and supplements.

Limitations: Blood magnesium can be normal even when body stores are low, because the body takes magnesium from bone to keep blood levels stable. A urine magnesium test or a red blood cell (RBC) magnesium test may add information; the RBC test may be better at finding low magnesium.
Because many different conditions can affect magnesium, an abnormal result is interpreted together with the medical history and other test results.

slides.title: Phosphate (inorganic phosphorus)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)

What it is used for: Used with other tests to help diagnose or monitor kidney disease (especially chronic kidney disease), bone disorders and parathyroid disorders. It may also be used to monitor people with poorly controlled diabetes or signs of an acid–base imbalance.

High or mildly low phosphate usually causes no symptoms on its own. Testing is often prompted by an abnormal calcium result, symptoms of low calcium, or symptoms of severely low phosphate, which can become life-threatening.

slides.title: Phosphate (inorganic phosphorus)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Phosphate contains the mineral phosphorus, so the test is also called a phosphorus test. Phosphate is an electrolyte the body needs to build strong bones and teeth (most body phosphate is in bone, combined with calcium), to make energy and for nerves and muscles to work properly.

Blood phosphate is controlled mainly by the kidneys and intestines and is linked to calcium (when calcium rises, phosphate falls, and vice versa), vitamin D and parathyroid hormone (PTH). To understand abnormal levels, phosphate is often tested together with calcium, vitamin D and PTH.

slides.title: Phosphate (inorganic phosphorus)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: High: High phosphate (hyperphosphatemia) is linked to late-stage chronic kidney disease and kidney failure, hypoparathyroidism (when PTH is low, calcium is low and phosphate is high), acidosis, and long-term use of certain medicines such as steroids, laxatives and phosphate-containing enemas.

slides.title: Phosphate (inorganic phosphorus)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Low: Mildly low phosphate (hypophosphatemia) is often not a health problem. Linked conditions include hyperparathyroidism (high calcium, low phosphate), vitamin D deficiency (which can lead to osteomalacia, or rickets in children), too little phosphorus from food (uncommon in the U.S.; more likely in premature babies and people with rare genetic disorders, severe malnutrition, alcohol use disorder or problems absorbing nutrients) and long-term use of antacids containing aluminum hydroxide or calcium carbonate and certain diuretics.

slides.title: Phosphate (inorganic phosphorus)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: Fasting for several hours may be required before the blood sample is taken. Tell the provider about all medicines (including over-the-counter ones), vitamins and supplements; prescription medicines should not be stopped unless the provider says so.
Interferences: Certain medicines, vitamins and supplements can affect the accuracy of phosphate results.

slides.title: Phosphate (inorganic phosphorus)
slides.eyebrow: Electrolytes and minerals · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: Reports may say “phosphorus” or “phosphate”; the terms mean the same thing. Interpretation depends on symptoms, medical history and other test results, and children often have higher levels because their bones are still growing. An abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Homeostasis and water balance
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 1/3
bullets: Homeostasis is the constancy of the internal environment (blood, lymph, cerebrospinal and interstitial fluid); it is largely determined by the content of water and minerals. Indicators of the internal environment: osmotic pressure, pH, acid–base balance.

slides.title: Homeostasis and water balance
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 2/3
bullets: Water is the most abundant substance in the body: about 50–60 % of body mass in adults (more in men, less in women); plentiful in blood, nervous tissue, muscle and liver, relatively scarce in connective tissue and bone.
Approximate daily balance: intake 2.5 L (fluids 1.2; food 1.0; endogenous water 0.3), output 2.5 L (urine 1.4; lungs 0.5; skin 0.5; stool 0.1).

slides.title: Homeostasis and water balance
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 3/3
bullets: The kidneys, lungs, skin, gastrointestinal tract and endocrine glands take part in water balance.

slides.title: Regulation of water balance and its disturbances
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 1/2
bullets: The main organ regulating water balance is the kidney: when water is short, urine is scanty and highly concentrated; when water is in excess, it is abundant and dilute. Loss of the kidney's ability to change urine concentration is seen in severe kidney disease.
Regulation rests on keeping osmotic pressure constant; the main system is the kidney and hormones: vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) and aldosterone.

Vasopressin secretion depends on plasma osmotic pressure: when pressure rises, secretion increases and reduces water loss through concentrated urine; once water is retained and pressure falls, secretion stops.

slides.title: Regulation of water balance and its disturbances
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 2/2
bullets: Aldosterone: when plasma sodium falls, its secretion rises and speeds up sodium reabsorption in the kidney (sodium is retained); when sodium rises, its production is suppressed.
Dehydration occurs with gastrointestinal disturbance, vomiting, profuse sweating, kidney disease and excessive salt intake.
An increase in extracellular fluid (polyhydria) shows as oedema; urine output falls (oliguria) or stops (anuria) — in kidney and liver disease.

slides.title: Role of minerals
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 1/2
bullets: Minerals are not an energy source but are indispensable and come only from food; their content in plant foods often depends on the soil (for example, iodine-poor soil is linked with endemic goitre).
Sodium, potassium and chloride: their main role is to maintain osmotic pressure; they activate enzymes and carry impulses along nervous tissue.

Calcium: a main component of bone; it takes part in nerve and muscle excitation, membrane permeability, muscle contraction and blood clotting. Deficiency disturbs bone formation and growth and can cause convulsions.
Phosphorus together with calcium builds bone tissue. Magnesium regulates neuromuscular excitability and heart function and activates many enzymes.

slides.title: Role of minerals
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 2/2
bullets: Trace elements (copper, zinc, manganese, iodine, cobalt, molybdenum and others) are needed in minute amounts; their importance lies mainly in activating enzyme systems or taking part in structures.

slides.title: A patient’s blood sodium is lower than normal. Which possible cause is consistent with the source?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Heart failure, which can make the body hold onto extra fluid
Dehydration from not drinking enough fluids over a long period
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source lists conditions that make the body hold onto fluid that dilutes sodium, including heart failure, as possible causes of low sodium.

Basis: Low sodium may reflect sodium loss or fluid retention that dilutes sodium; dehydration and diabetes insipidus are listed among causes of high sodium.

slides.title: A person without complaints has a sodium result slightly outside the normal range. Which statement best reflects the source?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Sodium varies widely in healthy people, so the result can be ignored
It does not necessarily mean disease: medicines, age, sex and some conditions can shift sodium, and the result is read together with other tests such as other electrolytes
It confirms kidney disease, because the kidneys control sodium
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source states that an out-of-range result does not always need treatment and that diagnosis uses other test results.

Basis: An out-of-range sodium result is interpreted in context: medicines, age, sex and other test results.

slides.title: A potassium result is unexpectedly high in a patient without complaints. Which collection-related factor named by the source could falsely raise it?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Not fasting for several hours before the test
Eating a lot of natural black licorice in the days leading up to the blood test
Repeated fist clenching and relaxing just before or during the blood draw
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source says this may temporarily increase potassium and lead to an incorrect result.

Basis: Fist clenching can temporarily raise potassium; licorice may lower it.

slides.title: Which of the following does the source list as a possible cause of LOW blood potassium?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Burns or surgery that make cells release potassium into the blood
Fluid loss from diarrhea, vomiting or heavy sweating
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source lists this as a possible cause of hypokalemia.

Basis: Causes of hypokalemia include diuretics, fluid loss, laxative overuse and adrenal disorders, among others.

slides.title: Which acid–base disturbance does the source link to LOW blood chloride?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Neither — chloride is unrelated to acid–base balance
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source lists metabolic alkalosis (too much base in the blood) as a possible cause of low chloride.

Basis: High chloride may go with metabolic acidosis; low chloride may go with metabolic alkalosis.

slides.title: A patient who takes antacids regularly has an abnormal chloride result. Which reading best follows the source?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Medicines such as antacids can cause abnormal chloride results, so medication use is considered when interpreting it
The result confirms kidney disease, whatever medicines the patient is taking
Antacids cannot change chloride results, so this abnormal value must reflect kidney or other disease that needs treatment
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source says certain medicines, such as antacids, can cause abnormal results.

Basis: Chloride results are interpreted taking medicines and fluid balance into account.

slides.title: Methods of determining sodium, potassium, chloride. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/3
bullets: 1. Sodium is the main extracellular cation (normal ~136–145 mmol/L), determines osmolality and volume; potassium is the main intracellular cation (~3.5–5.0 mmol/L), membrane potential, heart rhythm; chloride is the main anion, acid-base balance.

2. Method – ion-selective electrodes (ISE): direct (undiluted – blood gas analyzers) and indirect (diluted – large biochemistry analyzers); with indirect ISE, hyperlipidemia and hyperproteinemia give false hyponatremia.

slides.title: Methods of determining sodium, potassium, chloride. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/3
bullets: 3. Potassium preanalytics: hemolysis, fist clenching, prolonged tourniquet, K-EDTA contamination, thrombocytosis/leukocytosis (in serum) give false hyperkalemia – when in doubt remeasure in heparinized plasma; storage in the cold also raises K.
4. Hyponatremia: water excess (SIADH, heart/liver failure), Na loss (diuretics, vomiting, adrenal insufficiency); hypernatremia – water loss, diabetes insipidus.

slides.title: Methods of determining sodium, potassium, chloride. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 3/3
bullets: 5. Hyperkalemia: renal failure, hypoaldosteronism, drugs, cell breakdown, acidosis; hypokalemia: diuretics, vomiting/diarrhea, hyperaldosteronism, alkalosis.
6. Chloride: falls in metabolic alkalosis (vomiting), rises in hyperchloremic acidosis; used in interpreting the anion gap (Na − (Cl + HCO3)).

slides.title: Biological significance of water-electrolyte metabolism?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Water makes up ~60% of body weight in adults: ~2/3 inside cells, ~1/3 outside cells (interstitial and intravascular).
2. Water is a solvent and transport medium, thermoregulation, the medium of metabolic reactions.

3. Electrolytes: Na⁺ – the main cation of extracellular fluid (osmolality and volume), K⁺ – intracellular (membrane potential, neuromuscular excitability), Cl⁻ and HCO3⁻ – the main anions (acid-base balance), Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ – enzymes, contraction, hemostasis.

slides.title: Biological significance of water-electrolyte metabolism?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 4. Plasma osmolality (~275–295 mOsm/kg) is determined mainly by Na; oncotic pressure is provided by albumin.
5. Disorders: dehydration/overhydration, imbalance of sodium and potassium – neurological and cardiac complications; laboratory monitoring – electrolytes, osmolality, hematocrit, protein.

slides.title: Regulation of water-electrolyte metabolism?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Osmoregulation: hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense a rise in plasma osmolality → thirst and secretion of ADH (vasopressin) → via V2 receptors in the renal collecting ducts aquaporin-2 – water reabsorption.
2. Volume regulation: the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system – aldosterone in the distal nephron increases Na reabsorption and K excretion; its secretion is regulated by K⁺ level and the RAAS.
3. Natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP) – natriuresis and vasodilation when volume increases.
4. The kidney is the final effector organ: filtration, reabsorption, concentration.

slides.title: Regulation of water-electrolyte metabolism?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 5. Laboratory reflection: plasma and urine osmolality, Na, K, urine Na; ADH disorders – diabetes insipidus (urine dilute, hypernatremia), SIADH (hyponatremia, urine concentrated).
